nodes.name: cluster
nodes.summary: Root DDL table defining a Kafka cluster identity (name, timestamps) that every other storage table transitively references via foreign key.

nodes.name: consumer_group
nodes.summary: DDL table for Kafka consumer groups, scoped to a cluster with a unique (cluster, name) constraint.

nodes.name: producer
nodes.summary: DDL table representing a non-transactional idempotent Kafka producer scoped to a cluster.

nodes.name: scram_credential
nodes.summary: DDL table storing per-cluster SCRAM SASL credentials (salt, iterations, stored/server keys) for client authentication.

nodes.name: topic
nodes.summary: DDL table defining Kafka topics within a cluster, including partition count, replication factor, and internal-topic flag.

nodes.name: consumer_group_detail
nodes.summary: DDL table holding the serialized group membership/assignment detail and e-tag for a consumer group.

nodes.name: producer_epoch
nodes.summary: DDL table tracking the current epoch for an idempotent producer, used to detect and reject stale/fenced producers.

nodes.name: topic_configuration
nodes.summary: DDL table storing per-topic configuration key/value overrides (e.g. retention, cleanup policy).

nodes.name: topition
nodes.summary: DDL table representing a topic-partition (topition) pair, the core addressable unit records and offsets are stored against.

nodes.name: txn
nodes.summary: DDL table defining a Kafka transaction identity, linking a transactional id to its cluster and initiating producer.

nodes.name: virtual_topic
nodes.summary: DDL table for virtual topics keyed by an arbitrary key blob under a parent topic, used for schema-partitioned or key-derived topic variants.

nodes.name: consumer_offset
nodes.summary: DDL table storing committed consumer offsets per consumer group and topic-partition, including leader epoch and metadata.

nodes.name: header
nodes.summary: DDL table storing Kafka record headers (ordered key/value pairs) keyed to a specific record's topition and offset.

nodes.name: producer_detail
nodes.summary: DDL table tracking per-partition sequence numbers for a producer epoch, used to detect duplicate/out-of-order idempotent writes.

nodes.name: record
nodes.summary: DDL table holding the actual Kafka record payloads (key, value, timestamp, attributes) stored per topition and offset.

nodes.name: txn_detail
nodes.summary: DDL table tracking the lifecycle state (BEGIN/PREPARE_COMMIT/PREPARE_ABORT/COMMITTED/ABORTED) and timeout of a specific transaction/producer-epoch pairing.

nodes.name: watermark
nodes.summary: DDL table tracking the low and high watermark offsets for a topic-partition.

nodes.name: txn_offset_commit
nodes.summary: DDL table recording a transactional offset commit request tying a transaction detail to a consumer group and generation/member id.

nodes.name: txn_topition
nodes.summary: DDL join table recording which topic-partitions have been added to a given transaction (AddPartitionsToTxn).

nodes.name: txn_offset_commit_tp
nodes.summary: DDL table recording the per-topic-partition committed offset and metadata belonging to a transactional offset commit.

nodes.name: freelist_count.sql
nodes.summary: SQLite maintenance query that reads pragma_freelist_count() and pragma_page_size() to compute reclaimable space in the libSQL database file.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses SQLite table-valued pragma functions rather than a plain SELECT against a table.

nodes.name: policy_compact_compaction.sql
nodes.summary: Finds superseded record offsets for a given topic-partition and key that are older than a reference offset, used to identify records eligible for log-compaction removal.

nodes.name: policy_compact_delete.sql
nodes.summary: Deletes a single record row identified by topition and offset_id, the removal step applied to records superseded during log compaction.

nodes.name: policy_compact_distinct_k.sql
nodes.summary: Lists the distinct record keys present in a topic-partition, enumerating the keys the compaction policy must resolve to a single surviving offset each.

nodes.name: policy_compact_max_offset_id.sql
nodes.summary: Returns the highest (most recent) offset_id for a given key within a topic-partition, identifying the record that must be retained during compaction.

nodes.name: policy_compact_topitions.sql
nodes.summary: Joins topition, topic, cluster, and topic_configuration to list the partitions of topics configured with a compact cleanup.policy for a given cluster.

nodes.name: policy_delete.sql
nodes.summary: CTE-based query that identifies topics with a delete cleanup.policy and retention.ms configuration, computes which records exceed their retention window, and deletes those ancient records.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses three chained CTEs (deletion, retention, ancient) with a coalesce fallback for missing retention.ms, then a correlated tuple-based DELETE.

nodes.name: vacuum_into.sql
nodes.summary: SQLite VACUUM INTO statement that writes a compacted copy of the database to a target path, used for backup or reclaiming space after deletions.

nodes.name: record_fetch.sql
nodes.summary: Parameterized PostgreSQL query that fetches records for a topic partition starting from a given offset, accumulating a running byte total via a window function so the result set can be capped at a maximum fetch size (mirrors the Kafka Fetch API's byte-limit semantics).
nodes.languageNotes: Uses a CTE with a windowed `sum(...) over (order by offset_id)` to compute a running byte size per row, then filters on that running total in the outer query to enforce a max-bytes cap without a second pass.

nodes.name: record_fetch_keyed.sql
nodes.summary: Variant of the record fetch query that additionally filters records by an exact key match (compared as UTF-8 bytes), used for key-scoped record retrieval from a topic partition.
nodes.languageNotes: Identical windowed running-byte-total pattern to record_fetch.sql, with an added `r.k = convert_to($7, 'UTF-8')` predicate to scope results to a single record key.

nodes.name: topic_select_uuid.sql
nodes.summary: Looks up a topic (or virtual topic) by cluster name and UUID, returning its name, internal flag, partition count, and replication factor; unions the base topic table with the virtual_topic table to resolve schema-derived sub-topics.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses a UNION across `topic` and `virtual_topic` joins so a single UUID lookup transparently resolves either a real topic or a virtual (schema-keyed) topic, synthesizing the virtual topic's display name as `<topic>/<key>`.

nodes.name: consumer_group_delete.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL statement that deletes a consumer group row identified by cluster name and group name, resolved via a join subquery on cluster and consumer_group.

nodes.name: consumer_group_detail.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that fetches the e_tag and JSON detail blob for a consumer group, used to read group metadata with optimistic-concurrency versioning.

nodes.name: consumer_group_detail_delete_by_cg.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL statement that deletes the consumer_group_detail row for a given cluster and consumer group name, used when a group is removed.

nodes.name: consumer_group_detail_insert.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL upsert into consumer_group_detail that stores a new detail JSON blob and e_tag, guarded by an optimistic-concurrency check against the previous e_tag, returning the updated row.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE combined with a WHERE clause on the existing e_tag to implement compare-and-swap semantics for group metadata updates.

nodes.name: consumer_group_insert.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL upsert that creates or refreshes a consumer_group row for a given cluster and group name, updating last_updated on conflict.

nodes.name: consumer_group_select.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that lists the names of all consumer groups belonging to a given cluster.

nodes.name: consumer_group_select_by_name.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that fetches a single consumer group's name and its optional detail blob by cluster and group name, using a left join to tolerate groups without detail rows.

nodes.name: consumer_offset_delete_by_cg.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL statement that deletes all consumer_offset rows for a given consumer group, used when a consumer group is deleted.

nodes.name: consumer_offset_delete_by_topic.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL statement that deletes consumer_offset rows referencing any partition of a given topic, used when a topic is deleted.

nodes.name: consumer_offset_insert.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL upsert that records a consumer group's committed offset, leader epoch, timestamp, and metadata for a specific topic-partition.

nodes.name: consumer_offset_insert_from_txn.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL upsert that commits consumer offsets from a completed Kafka transaction by joining producer, producer_epoch, txn, txn_detail, txn_offset_commit, and txn_offset_commit_tp tables into consumer_offset.
nodes.languageNotes: Multi-table join across the transactional coordinator schema (txn/txn_detail/txn_offset_commit) reflects Kafka's transactional offset-commit protocol implemented on top of relational storage.

nodes.name: consumer_offset_select.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that fetches the committed offset for a consumer group on a specific topic-partition.

nodes.name: consumer_offset_select_by_group.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that lists topic name, partition, and committed offset for every topic-partition a consumer group has committed offsets on.

nodes.name: header_copy.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL COPY FROM STDIN BINARY statement that bulk-loads record header rows (topition, offset_id, ordinal, key, value) into the header table for high-throughput writes.
nodes.languageNotes: COPY BINARY is used instead of row-by-row INSERTs to minimize per-record overhead when persisting record headers at high produce throughput.

nodes.name: header_delete_by_topic.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL statement that deletes header rows belonging to records of a given topic, matching both topition and offset_id via correlated subqueries, used when a topic is deleted.

nodes.name: header_fetch.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that fetches the ordered key/value headers attached to a single record identified by topic, partition, and offset.

nodes.name: header_insert.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL statement that inserts a single header key/value pair, with its ordinal position, for a record identified by topic, partition, and offset.

nodes.name: list_earliest_offset.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that returns the earliest (log-start) record offset and its timestamp for a given topic-partition.

nodes.name: list_latest_offset_committed.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that computes the last-stable-offset (LSO) for a topic-partition by taking the minimum between active transactions' initial offsets and the high watermark, implementing Kafka's read-committed isolation semantics.
nodes.languageNotes: Combines two unioned subqueries (in-flight transaction start offsets and the watermark-derived high offset minus one) then orders and limits to one row, mirroring the LSO definition described in the file's own comments.

nodes.name: list_latest_offset_timestamp.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that finds the earliest record offset whose timestamp is greater than or equal to a given timestamp, used to implement time-based offset lookup (offsetsForTimes).

nodes.name: list_latest_offset_uncommitted.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query that returns the next offset and timestamp available for a partition by joining cluster, topic, topition, watermark, and record, used to find the latest uncommitted offset.

nodes.name: maintain-vacuum.sql
nodes.summary: SQLite/libSQL maintenance query that reads the pragma_freelist_count and pragma_page_size pragmas to estimate reclaimable free space ahead of a VACUUM.

nodes.name: policy_compact.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres compaction query that deletes superseded record versions for topics whose cleanup.policy is 'compact', keeping only the highest offset per key via CTE-based duplicate detection.

nodes.name: policy_delete.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres retention query that deletes records older than a topic's retention.ms (or a supplied default) for topics whose cleanup.policy is 'delete', computed via CTEs over topic configuration and timestamps.

nodes.name: producer_detail_delete_by_topic.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres delete statement that removes all producer_detail rows (per-partition idempotent-producer sequence state) for every partition of a named topic.

nodes.name: producer_detail_insert.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres upsert that records or increments the per-partition sequence number tracked for an idempotent producer's epoch, enforcing exactly-once produce semantics.

nodes.name: producer_epoch_current_for_producer.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query returning the most recent epoch assigned to a given producer within a named cluster.

nodes.name: producer_epoch_for_current_txn.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query resolving the producer id, current epoch, and transaction status for a named transaction by joining producer, producer_epoch, txn, and txn_detail.

nodes.name: producer_epoch_insert.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres statement that computes the next monotonically increasing epoch for a producer via a CTE and inserts it into producer_epoch, returning the new epoch for producer fencing.

nodes.name: producer_insert.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres insert that registers a new producer row scoped to a named cluster and returns its generated id.

nodes.name: producer_select_for_update.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query that resolves a producer's current per-partition sequence number, defaulting to zero when no producer_detail row exists yet, used to validate incoming record sequence numbers.

nodes.name: producer_update_epoch_with_txn.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres update that bumps a producer's epoch and resets its sequence counter for a named transaction, returning the producer's new id and epoch.

nodes.name: producer_update_sequence.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres update that advances a producer's sequence counter by a given delta for a specific producer/epoch pair.

nodes.name: record_copy.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres COPY statement enabling bulk binary ingestion of records (offset, attributes, producer id/epoch, timestamp, key, value) into the record table for high-throughput produce paths.

nodes.name: record_delete_by_topic.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres delete statement that removes all record rows across every partition of a named topic, used when a topic is deleted.

nodes.name: record_fetch.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres fetch query returning records for a partition starting at a given offset, capped by a maximum byte budget computed via a running-sum window function, powering the Kafka Fetch API.

nodes.name: record_fetch_keyed.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres fetch query variant that additionally filters records by a specific key, reusing the same byte-budget window function as record_fetch, for compacted/keyed reads.

nodes.name: record_insert.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres insert that appends a new record to the correct topition (partition) for a named cluster and topic, with values supplied by the produce path.

nodes.name: register_broker.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres upsert that registers or refreshes a cluster/broker entry by name, bumping its last_updated timestamp on conflict during broker startup registration.

nodes.name: scram_credential_delete.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres delete statement that removes a SCRAM SASL credential for a given username and mechanism scoped to a named cluster.

nodes.name: scram_credential_insert
nodes.summary: Postgres upsert query that inserts a SASL/SCRAM credential (salt, iterations, stored/server keys) for a cluster, username, and mechanism, updating the existing row on conflict.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses `on conflict (cluster, username, mechanism) do update` for an atomic upsert keyed by the composite SCRAM credential identity.

nodes.name: scram_credential_select
nodes.summary: Postgres query that looks up the salt, iteration count, and stored/server keys for a SASL/SCRAM credential by cluster name, username, and mechanism.

nodes.name: topic_by_cluster
nodes.summary: Postgres query that lists all topics (uuid, name, internal flag, partitions, replication factor) belonging to a named cluster.

nodes.name: topic_by_uuid
nodes.summary: Postgres query that fetches a single topic's metadata by cluster name and topic uuid.

nodes.name: topic_configuration_delete
nodes.summary: Postgres query that deletes a single named topic configuration entry, scoped to a topic identified by cluster and topic name.

nodes.name: topic_configuration_delete_by_topic
nodes.summary: Postgres query that removes all configuration entries for a topic identified by cluster and topic name, used when a topic's config is reset or the topic is deleted.

nodes.name: topic_configuration_select
nodes.summary: Postgres query that returns all name/value configuration pairs for a topic identified by cluster and topic name.

nodes.name: topic_configuration_upsert
nodes.summary: Postgres upsert query that sets a topic's named configuration value, inserting a new row or updating the existing one on conflict and returning the row id.

nodes.name: topic_delete_by
nodes.summary: Postgres query that deletes a topic row identified by cluster name and topic name, used when a topic is deleted from the broker.

nodes.name: topic_insert
nodes.summary: Postgres query that creates a new topic row (name, uuid, partitions, replication factor) under a named cluster and returns the generated topic uuid.

nodes.name: topic_select
nodes.summary: Postgres query that resolves the internal row id of a topic given cluster name and topic name, typically used before joining to related tables.

nodes.name: topic_select_name
nodes.summary: Postgres query that fetches a topic's metadata (uuid, internal flag, partitions, replication factor) by cluster name and topic name.

nodes.name: topic_select_uuid
nodes.summary: Postgres query that resolves a topic or virtual topic by uuid within a cluster, unioning matches from the topic table with matches from the virtual_topic table.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses a UNION across `topic` and `virtual_topic` so a single uuid lookup transparently resolves either a real or a virtual (derived) topic.

nodes.name: topition_delete_by_topic
nodes.summary: Postgres query that deletes all topic-partition (topition) rows belonging to a topic identified by cluster and topic name.

nodes.name: topition_insert
nodes.summary: Postgres query that creates a new topic-partition (topition) row for a given cluster, topic name, and partition number, returning the generated row id.

nodes.name: topition_select
nodes.summary: Postgres query that fetches topic metadata for a specific partition, joining topic and topition by cluster name, topic name, and partition number.

nodes.name: topition_select_id
nodes.summary: Postgres query that resolves the internal row id of a topic-partition (topition) given cluster name, topic name, and partition number.

nodes.name: txn_detail_insert
nodes.summary: Postgres query that records a new transaction detail row linking a named transaction to a producer's epoch, with a timeout, for Kafka transactional produce support.

nodes.name: txn_detail_select
nodes.summary: Postgres query that reads the current epoch and sequence for a producer's transaction detail row, taking a row lock (FOR NO KEY UPDATE) to serialize concurrent transactional writers.
nodes.languageNotes: `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` takes a row-level lock without blocking foreign-key-referencing inserts, used to guard concurrent transactional produce paths.

nodes.name: txn_detail_select_current
nodes.summary: Postgres query that returns each producer's current epoch and latest transaction status for a named transaction within a cluster, grouped by producer.

nodes.name: txn_detail_select_for_update.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that locks a transaction's `txn_detail` row (`FOR NO KEY UPDATE`) keyed by cluster, transaction name, producer id, and producer epoch, returning its epoch, sequence, and status for the transactional coordinator.

nodes.name: txn_detail_select_status_for_update.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that locks the `txn_detail` row via `FOR UPDATE` and reads its status, preventing a racing EndTxn or abort sweep from double-finalizing the same transaction.
nodes.languageNotes: Explicit row locking (FOR UPDATE) is used to serialize concurrent finalization attempts on the same transaction.

nodes.name: txn_detail_select_timed_out.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query used by the abort sweep to find transactions still in the BEGIN state whose elapsed time (computed against a passed-in `now` timestamp) exceeds their configured transaction timeout.
nodes.languageNotes: Computes elapsed time via timestamptz subtraction so the comparison is independent of session timezone.

nodes.name: txn_detail_update_sequence.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that increments the producer sequence counter on a `txn_detail` row for a given cluster, transaction, producer, and epoch.

nodes.name: txn_detail_update_started_at.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that (re)starts a transaction by setting `txn_detail.started_at` and status to BEGIN, guarded to only reset a fresh row or one whose prior transaction already resolved (COMMITTED/ABORTED), never one still in flight.
nodes.languageNotes: The guard clause encodes an invariant that status alone (not started_at) determines whether a txn_detail row is reusable, avoiding a redundant started_at check.

nodes.name: txn_insert.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that inserts a new `txn` row (cluster, transaction name, producer) resolved from the cluster name, registering a new transactional id for a producer.

nodes.name: txn_offset_commit_delete_by_txn.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that deletes all `txn_offset_commit` rows belonging to a specific transaction, cluster, producer, and producer epoch, used when finalizing or cleaning up a transaction's pending offset commits.

nodes.name: txn_offset_commit_insert.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that records a consumer group offset commit staged inside a transaction, inserting a `txn_offset_commit` row linked to the transaction's `txn_detail` and the consumer group.

nodes.name: txn_offset_commit_tp_delete_by_topic.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that deletes per-partition `txn_offset_commit_tp` rows for every `topition` of a named topic, used when a topic (and its partitions) is removed.

nodes.name: txn_offset_commit_tp_delete_by_txn.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that deletes per-partition `txn_offset_commit_tp` rows tied to a specific transaction, cluster, producer, and producer epoch.

nodes.name: txn_offset_commit_tp_insert.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that inserts a per-partition committed offset (`txn_offset_commit_tp`) for a consumer group's transactional offset commit, resolving the topic partition and offset-commit row from cluster, transaction, group, producer, and topic/partition identifiers.

nodes.name: txn_produce_offset_delete_by_topic.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that deletes `txn_produce_offset` rows for every topition of a named topic, used when a topic is deleted so no stale transactional produce-offset tracking remains.

nodes.name: txn_produce_offset_delete_by_txn.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that deletes `txn_produce_offset` rows for a specific transaction, producer, and producer epoch, carefully scoped to that epoch alone so it doesn't wipe offset tracking for other epochs of the same producer.
nodes.languageNotes: Comment explains a subtle correctness requirement: joining on producer_epoch is mandatory since txn_detail rows are reused across a producer's sequential transactions after reconnects.

nodes.name: txn_produce_offset_insert.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL upsert that records the produced offset range for a topic-partition within a transaction, inserting or updating a `txn_produce_offset` row keyed by `txn_topition` with `offset_end` and `last_updated` refreshed on conflict.

nodes.name: txn_produce_offset_select_offset_range.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that reads the produced offset start/end range for a topic-partition within a specific transaction, producer, and producer epoch.

nodes.name: txn_produce_offset_select_overlapping_txn.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that finds other resolved transactions whose produced offsets on a topic-partition overlap a given offset boundary, used to detect conflicting concurrent transactions on the same partition via a SELECT/EXCEPT pattern excluding the current transaction, ordered by offset_end.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses SQL EXCEPT between two structurally identical SELECTs to subtract the current transaction from the set of overlapping ones.

nodes.name: txn_select_name.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that resolves a transaction's producer id from the cluster name and transaction name.

nodes.name: txn_select_produced_topitions.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that lists every topic/partition a transaction produced to, deterministically ordered by topic name then partition so that callers taking per-partition watermark locks (during transaction finalization) always acquire them in a consistent order and avoid deadlocks.
nodes.languageNotes: Deterministic ORDER BY is a correctness requirement here, not a cosmetic choice: it prevents lock-ordering deadlocks between concurrently finalizing transactions.

nodes.name: txn_select_producer_epoch.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that resolves a transaction's current producer id and producer epoch from the cluster and transaction names.

nodes.name: txn_status_update.sql
nodes.summary: PostgreSQL query that updates a `txn_detail` row's status and `last_updated` timestamp for a given cluster, transaction, producer, and producer epoch, used to transition a transaction between states (e.g., PREPARE_COMMIT, COMMITTED, ABORTED).

nodes.name: txn_topition_delete_by_topic.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query that deletes all txn_topition rows for every partition of a named topic, used when a topic is deleted so transaction-partition registrations don't leak.

nodes.name: txn_topition_delete_by_txn.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query that removes txn_topition rows belonging to one specific (transaction, producer, producer epoch) combination, carefully scoped by epoch so it doesn't wipe registrations from other epochs of the same producer.
nodes.languageNotes: Comment explains a subtle correctness requirement: joining on producer_epoch.id (not just producer id) prevents deleting txn_topition rows across all epochs of a reused (transaction_id, producer_id) pair.

nodes.name: txn_topition_insert.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query implementing Kafka's AddPartitionsToTxn: idempotently registers a topic partition against an active transaction via ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING so retries and racing produces don't fail on a unique violation.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses `on conflict (txn_detail, topition) do nothing` to make the Kafka AddPartitionsToTxn semantics idempotent at the SQL level.

nodes.name: txn_topition_select.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query that reads the produce offset range (offset_start, offset_end) recorded for a partition within an active transaction, keyed by cluster/producer/epoch/topic/partition.

nodes.name: txn_topition_select_txns.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query that counts distinct transaction names currently referencing a given topic partition, used to detect whether a partition has active transactional writers.

nodes.name: virtual_topic_upsert.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres upsert query that creates or refreshes a virtual_topic mapping (topic, key -> uuid) for a cluster/topic, updating last_updated on conflict and returning the resolved uuid.

nodes.name: watermark_delete_by_topic.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query that deletes watermark rows for every partition of a named topic, used to clean up low/high offset tracking when a topic is deleted.

nodes.name: watermark_insert.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query that creates a new watermark row for a topic partition, returning the generated watermark id, used when a partition is first created.

nodes.name: watermark_insert_from_txn.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres upsert query that seeds or updates a partition's stable (last-stable-offset) watermark field from a transaction's produce offset end, keyed by cluster/transaction/producer/epoch.

nodes.name: watermark_select.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query that reads a partition's low/high watermark alongside a CTE-computed stable offset derived from the minimum start offset across its still-active (prepare/begin) transactions, implementing Kafka's last-stable-offset semantics.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses a `with stable as (...)` CTE joined with a LEFT JOIN so partitions with no active transactions still return a row with a null stable offset.

nodes.name: watermark_select_for_update.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query that reads a partition's low/high watermark with a `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` row lock, used to serialize concurrent watermark mutations within a transaction.
nodes.languageNotes: `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` locks the row against concurrent updates/deletes while still permitting non-conflicting key-share locks, weaker (and more concurrency-friendly) than a plain `FOR UPDATE`.

nodes.name: watermark_select_no_update.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query that reads a partition's low/high watermark without taking a row lock, the lightweight read path for callers that don't need to mutate the watermark afterward.

nodes.name: watermark_select_stable.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query that computes the last stable offset for a partition directly as the minimum produce-offset-start across its active transactions, used for last-stable-offset (LSO) tracking as described in the header comment.
nodes.languageNotes: Header comment documents the Kafka LSO invariant: the last stable offset equals the minimum of the initial offsets across all active transactions.

nodes.name: watermark_update.sql
nodes.summary: Postgres query that updates a partition's low/high watermark bounds and last_updated timestamp, the primary mutation used after appends or truncations change the partition's offset range.

nodes.name: header_default

nodes.name: producer

nodes.name: producer_epoch

nodes.name: administrator.rs
nodes.summary: Core consumer-group coordination state machine: implements the typestate `Group` trait (Forming/Formed), the `Wrapper`/`Inner` runtime representation of a group, and `Controller`, the `Coordinator` implementation that dispatches join/sync/heartbeat/leave/offset-commit/offset-fetch requests against pluggable storage.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses a typestate pattern (`Inner<O, Forming>` / `Inner<O, Formed>`) so the compiler enforces that group-lifecycle operations are only valid in the appropriate protocol state; `Wrapper<O>` erases the state generic for storage at runtime.

nodes.name: Group
nodes.summary: Async trait defining the consumer-group lifecycle operations (join, sync, heartbeat, leave, offset_commit, offset_fetch) with associated per-operation state types, implemented separately for the Forming and Formed typestates.

nodes.name: Wrapper
nodes.summary: Enum erasing the Forming/Formed typestate so a group can be stored and looked up at runtime, converting to and from the persisted `GroupDetail` representation.

nodes.name: Controller
nodes.summary: Top-level group coordinator holding the storage handle and an in-memory map of active groups (`WrapperMap`); implements the `Coordinator` trait used by the broker's group request handlers.

nodes.name: Forming
nodes.summary: Typestate marker for a consumer group that has not yet completed a rebalance, tracking the candidate protocol type/name and leader.

nodes.name: Formed
nodes.summary: Typestate marker for a consumer group that has completed a rebalance, holding the agreed protocol, leader, and per-member partition assignments.

nodes.name: Inner
nodes.summary: Generic group state container (`Inner<O, S>`) holding members, generation id, timeouts, storage handle, and the typestate `S`; the concrete type behind both `Forming` and `Formed` groups.

nodes.name: Member
nodes.summary: Per-member group state: the member's cached JoinGroupResponse fragment and the timestamp of its last contact, used for heartbeat-timeout detection.

nodes.name: from
nodes.summary: Converts a `&Wrapper<O>` into the storage-layer `GroupDetail` snapshot used to persist group state.

nodes.name: with_storage_group_detail
nodes.summary: Rehydrates a `Wrapper<O>` from a persisted `GroupDetail` plus a storage handle, reconstructing either the Forming or Formed state, used when a group is loaded back from storage.

nodes.name: members
nodes.summary: Returns the current member set of a wrapped group, delegating to whichever inner state (Forming or Formed) is active.

nodes.name: is_ok
nodes.summary: Checks whether a group response body's error code indicates success, used to gate leader-only or member-validation logic.

nodes.name: is_assigned
nodes.summary: Determines whether a join/sync response already carries a partition assignment for the calling member.

nodes.name: missed_heartbeat
nodes.summary: Checks whether a member of a Forming group has exceeded its session timeout since its last contact, used to expire stale members before a rebalance completes.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Nisshi is a stateless, Apache Kafka-compatible broker written in Rust that swaps Kafka's usual storage layer for pluggable backends: PostgreSQL, libSQL/SQLite, S3/object store, or plain memory. The README frames the project's core bet: because the broker holds no local state, any of these backends can serve as the durable source of truth, and schema-validated topics (Avro, JSON Schema, Protobuf) can additionally be written out as Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake tables. It also introduces the single binary's five subcommands (broker, topic, cat, proxy, generator/perf) that the rest of this tour will trace through the code.

tour.title: The 15-Crate Workspace
tour.description: Before diving into code, this workspace manifest shows how Nisshi's concerns are physically separated: one crate per architectural responsibility (broker, storage, schema, wire protocol, network service, CLI, client) rather than one large monolith. This decomposition is what lets `nisshi-sans-io` stay a pure, dependency-light protocol crate while `nisshi-storage` carries all the database-specific code, and it's why features like `postgres` or `iceberg` can be compiled in or out independently. Keep this crate map in mind as later steps jump between `nisshi-broker`, `nisshi-service`, `nisshi-storage`, and `nisshi-schema`.

tour.title: Application Entry Point
tour.description: This is the thinnest possible binary: it loads `.env`, wires up OpenTelemetry tracing, and immediately hands control to `Cli::main()` in the `nisshi-cli` crate. Putting almost no logic in the binary crate itself is a deliberate Rust idiom, it keeps the actual behavior in library crates that are independently testable and reusable, and it means this file barely ever needs to change even as subcommands are added.
tour.languageLesson: Rust workspaces commonly separate a tiny `src/bin/*.rs` binary crate from the library crates that hold the real logic. This keeps compile times down for the binary and lets other crates (or tests) depend on the library code without linking a full executable.

tour.title: CLI Subcommand Dispatch
tour.description: Building on Step 3's handoff, this file defines the `Cli` struct and its seven subcommands (Broker, Cat, Generator, Perf, Proxy, Topic, User) using `clap`'s derive macros, then dispatches each variant to its own async `main()`. This is the fork in the road that decides whether the process becomes a long-running broker, a one-shot topic-management CLI, or a producer/consumer tool, all from the same compiled binary.
tour.languageLesson: Clap's `#[derive(Subcommand)]` turns a Rust enum into a full CLI subcommand tree with help text and argument parsing generated at compile time, avoiding hand-written argument-matching boilerplate.

tour.title: Bootstrapping the Broker
tour.description: When the `broker` subcommand is chosen, `cli/broker.rs` parses listener, storage-URL, schema-registry, TLS, and data-lake options and uses them to construct a fully configured `Broker`. That construction bottoms out in `nisshi-broker/src/broker.rs`, which defines the `Broker` struct's lifecycle: startup, the TCP accept loop, periodic maintenance sweeps, and graceful shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM. This is the seam between CLI configuration (Step 4) and the broker's actual runtime behavior.

tour.title: Generic Broker: Coordinator + Storage
tour.description: `nisshi-broker` is built around `Broker<G, S>`, generic over a Coordinator type `G` and a Storage type `S`, which is how the same broker logic runs unmodified against any storage backend or coordination strategy. `coordinator.rs` wraps a concrete `Coordinator` implementation as a rama Service/Layer, and `coordinator/group.rs` declares the `Coordinator` trait itself: join, sync, heartbeat, leave, and offset commit/fetch, the core Kafka consumer-group protocol. This generic design is central to Nisshi's pitch of a stateless broker: the group-coordination logic is written once and reused no matter which storage engine from Step 9 backs it.
tour.languageLesson: Generic type parameters like `Broker<G, S>` let Rust monomorphize the broker at compile time for each concrete Coordinator/Storage pair, giving the flexibility of an interface with none of the runtime cost of dynamic dispatch.

tour.title: Network Service Layers (rama)
tour.description: Every TCP connection into the broker passes through a stack of composable `rama` Layers and Services: `stream.rs` implements the outermost TCP accept loop and raw length-prefixed frame I/O, while `frame.rs` and `api.rs` carry a decoded Kafka `Frame` through authentication, request/response typing, and routing to the correct per-API-key handler. This Layer/Service composition pattern (`TcpBytesLayer` -> `BytesFrameLayer` -> `FrameRouteService` -> `FrameBytesLayer` -> `BytesTcpService`) is reused for the broker, the proxy, and the CLI client alike, so understanding it here pays off across the whole codebase.
tour.languageLesson: The Layer/Service pattern (borrowed from the `tower` ecosystem) wraps a base Service in successive middleware Layers, each adding one concern (framing, auth, routing) without the layers below needing to know about the ones above.

tour.title: Kafka Wire Protocol Codegen
tour.description: `nisshi-sans-io` supplies the typed Rust structs that `frame.rs` (Step 7) serializes and deserializes on the wire. Rather than hand-writing ~185 request/response types, `build.rs` reads Apache Kafka's own JSON message descriptors at compile time and generates versioned, tagged-field-aware structs with `Serialize`/`Deserialize` derived automatically; `lib.rs` supplies the shared scaffolding (ApiKey registry, Frame envelope, error codes, compression codecs) those generated types build on. Because this crate does no I/O of its own, it can be reused unchanged by the broker, the client, and the proxy.
tour.languageLesson: "Sans-I/O" is a design pattern where a protocol library implements only encoding/decoding logic, with zero knowledge of sockets or async runtimes. It maximizes reuse and testability since the same types work whether the caller is sync, async, in-process, or fuzzing raw bytes.

tour.title: Storage Abstraction & Backends
tour.description: `nisshi-storage`'s `lib.rs` defines the `Storage` trait plus the `StorageContainer` enum that dispatches every broker operation (produce, fetch, offsets, groups, transactions) to a concrete backend selected at runtime from a URL like `postgres://` or `sqlite://`. `pg.rs` and `lite.rs` are two of those backends: both implement the same trait as prepared SQL statements, but `pg.rs` targets a pooled PostgreSQL connection with Iceberg/Delta write integration while `lite.rs` wraps a local SQLite `Delegate` behind a channel-based `Engine`. This is the concrete realization of the `S` type parameter from Step 6, and it's why Nisshi can be "the same broker" no matter which storage engine backs it.
tour.languageLesson: `StorageContainer` uses enum dispatch rather than a boxed `dyn Storage` trait object: each backend variant is matched explicitly, which avoids virtual-call overhead and lets the compiler flag any backend that doesn't implement every required operation.

tour.title: The PostgreSQL Schema
tour.description: This DDL script is what `pg.rs` from Step 9 actually talks to: 23 tables covering clusters, topics/partitions, records and headers, consumer groups/offsets, producer epochs, transactions, and SCRAM credentials, plus 15 supporting views. Because Nisshi's broker is stateless, this schema effectively is the durable state of a Postgres-backed cluster, every `Topition` and `GroupDetail` type referenced in `nisshi-storage/src/lib.rs` maps directly to rows defined here.
tour.languageLesson: Initdb scripts like this run once when a fresh PostgreSQL container starts. Because Nisshi supports multiple storage engines behind one trait, this schema has to encode Kafka-specific concepts (topics, partitions, consumer group offsets) that have no native SQL equivalent, which is why it leans on companion views to keep query call sites simple.

tour.title: Schema Registry & Format Validation
tour.description: Alongside raw byte storage, Nisshi can validate topic records against a schema before they're written. `nisshi-schema/src/lib.rs` defines the `Schema` enum and shared `Validator`/`Generator` traits, while `avro.rs` and `proto.rs` are two concrete backends: Avro schema parsing/validation/conversion, and Protobuf file-descriptor-based encode/decode/validate (with a Rhai scripting engine for generating sample messages). This is the registry the README's `--schema-registry file://` and `s3://` examples point at, and it feeds directly into the data-lake writers in the next step.
tour.languageLesson: Protobuf field numbers are permanent once shipped: a compatible schema evolution can only add new optional fields, never reuse or renumber a deleted one. `proto.rs` builds descriptors dynamically at runtime specifically so it can validate against whatever `.proto` file a topic was configured with, rather than requiring compiled-in message types.

tour.title: Writing to the Data Lake
tour.description: Once a record passes schema validation (Step 11), it can optionally be written to a data lake table instead of, or alongside, the broker's own storage. `lake.rs` defines the `House` enum and `LakeHouse` trait unifying three backends, and `lake/berg.rs` and `lake/delta.rs` implement two of them: Iceberg via a REST catalog client that creates namespaces/tables on demand, and Delta Lake via DataFusion and delta-rs with partitioning, z-ordering, and optimize/compaction maintenance. This is what turns Nisshi from "a Kafka broker" into "a Kafka broker that can also populate your analytics lakehouse", the feature the README leads with.

tour.title: Containerization & Local Dev Stack
tour.description: The Dockerfile packages the `nisshi` binary from Step 3 into a production image: a multi-stage, cross-compiling build using the `tonistiigi/xx` toolchain on Rust/Alpine statically links against musl, then copies only the resulting binary into a minimal `scratch` image with CA certificates, keeping the runtime image tiny with no shell or package manager to attack. `compose.yaml` is the local-dev counterpart, wiring up the same broker alongside PostgreSQL, MinIO (S3), Grafana, Jaeger, Prometheus, and a Lakekeeper Iceberg catalog, so every backend from Steps 9-12 has something real to talk to during development.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker builds use one `FROM` stage with the full compiler toolchain and a second, minimal `FROM scratch` (or Alpine) stage that copies in only the finished artifact. Combined with static musl linking, this produces a container with no dynamic libc dependency and a dramatically smaller attack surface than a typical distro-based runtime image.

tour.title: CI/CD Pipeline
tour.description: The GitHub Actions workflow ties every earlier step together as an automated gate: check, fmt, and clippy run first, then the workspace is built independently per storage feature and per storage+lake feature combination (validating the feature-flag isolation from Step 2), then the full nextest suite runs against a PostgreSQL 16/17/18 matrix, followed by librdkafka and franz-go client compatibility tests and a multi-arch Docker packaging job that runs Java Kafka client smoke tests against the exact image built in Step 13. This is the capstone that proves the crate boundaries, storage backends, and container build all actually work together before a change ships.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions workflows use `jobs` for parallel work and `steps` for sequential execution within a job; a matrix strategy (like the PostgreSQL 16/17/18 versions here) runs the same job definition once per matrix value, catching version-specific regressions without duplicating YAML.
